opening.headline: When starting quickly with an administrative search approach, when departmental permission segregation requirements arise, evaluate the trade-off between operational burden and control level to determine the appropriate method.
body: The fastest way to address document search needs is through a managed search solution where, upon uploading files, the system automatically performs segmentation, embedding, indexing, and searching—tasks handled by the provider rather than the user. This approach is sufficient initially. However, as the service scales, requirements emerge such as restricting HR documents to HR staff only and financial documents to the finance team only, and users begin to desire more granular control over segmentation and logging.

In this class, we examine how much responsibility management-based file search takes on, and how RAG engines and custom-built solutions are composed. We then compare operational responsibilities and control levels item by item, and provide an explanation of how to determine the appropriate approach for document access separation by department.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the composition and operational overhead of managed search versus directly built RAG.
Can determine an appropriate approach that aligns with authorization separation and customization requirements

screens.title: We started with a managed approach, but requirements for privilege separation emerged.
screens.lead: Read the following scenario and consider what aspect might cause you to reconsider your approach.

visual.alt: A scene where personnel, financial, and sales documents are mixed in a single document repository, and users from all three departments access the same search interface.

paragraphs: A team quickly implemented an internal document Q&A service using managed search. Providers only needed to upload files, with the rest handled automatically, making development and operations lightweight. All documents were centralized in one location, and all employees used the same search functionality.

Then the requirements changed. They want HR documents to be accessible only to the HR team and financial documents only to the finance team. Documents from other departments must not be mixed in the search results. While the managed approach is convenient, it limits the scope of control over internal operations. On the other hand, if we move to a fully custom-built solution, we gain greater control, but we also take on full operational responsibility—including segmentation, embedding, indexing, searching, updating, and incident response.

Ultimately, the choice is not about which option is better, but rather how much control you're willing to accept in exchange for how much operational responsibility you'll bear. This course examines that trade-off through specific examples.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Is departmental separation about where to place documents, or about filtering what to retrieve during searches? This distinction is made in the case study explanation of the class.

screens.outro: First, let's recall the points that were disappointing when using managed search.

screens.title: Recall whether you've experienced the limitations of managed search.
screens.lead: When you select a point, the instructor's thoughts are presented. Since you haven't entered or submitted an answer, first recall whether you've had a similar experience.

items.prompt: Have you ever wanted to change the size or method of splitting a document?
items.answer: The partitioning approach directly affects search quality. Managed modes also provide some level of control. For example, Gemini File Search offers settings to specify the maximum number of tokens per chunk and the number of overlapping tokens. However, the adjustable options are limited to the range opened by the provider.

items.prompt: Have you ever had to filter search results on a per-user basis?
items.answer: Permission separation is the most common trigger. OpenAI file search provides a metadata filter that allows filtering based on properties when searching within vector store files. If the scope defined by this filter can be resolved through a managed approach, then the scope remains within bounds; however, if direct integration with internal permission systems is required, the scope extends beyond this.

items.prompt: Have you ever wanted to see more detailed cost or log information?
items.answer: In a managed approach, processing occurs within the provider's environment, so you may not be able to view intermediate logs and metrics to the extent you desire. In a self-built setup, you can directly measure each step, but you also end up being responsible for monitoring and incident response.

screens.outro: Let's verify the scope of services managed by the managed type with the two companies' services.

screens.title: Managed file search: Scope assigned
screens.lead: Select each tab to examine what company-specific managed file searches handle instead. The last tab summarizes the commonalities.

tabs.label: Gemini File Search
tabs.body: The Gemini API's File Search tool retrieves files, splits them into chunks, and indexes them, then searches for relevant information matching the prompt and injects it into the model's context. Generating embeddings at the time of file storage and querying is free, and incurs only the cost of embedding generation when initially indexing the file and standard model input/output token charges. You can use the default splitting method, but specify the maximum tokens per chunk and overlapping tokens using `chunking_config`. Responses include source information in the file_citation format.

tabs.label: OpenAI file search
tabs.body: OpenAI's file search is a hosting tool managed by OpenAI. Once a vector store is created and files are uploaded, the files are automatically split, embedded, and indexed. When the tool list includes file_search and the vector store during a model call, the model will invoke them when needed to perform semantic and keyword searches. Reducing the number of results retrieved with max_num_results can lower token usage and latency, but may degrade the quality of the answers. Storage costs are billed based on the size of the parsed fragments and their embeddings.

tabs.label: common ground
tabs.body: Both services manage only files and storage, while the provider is responsible for partitioning, embedding, indexing, and search algorithms. Responses include file citation information to provide evidence, and there is no need to operate a separate search server. On the other hand, most internal operations default to provider-supplied settings, so requirements beyond this scope cannot be met through configuration. This boundary defines the limit for direct construction.

screens.outro: Now, let's examine the components that are being assembled directly rather than being handed over.

screens.title: RAG engine and directly built RAG components
screens.lead: When an item is selected, a description of the corresponding configuration is displayed. As you move from top to bottom, the number of parts that can be directly chosen and managed increases.

items.title: RAG Engine: Framework that groups stages in a managed manner
items.body: The RAG Engine is a service that provides a managed configuration for six stages: collection, transformation (chunking), embedding, indexing, searching, and generation. Indexing is created at the corpus level and can be analogized to a detailed table of contents of a comprehensive reference work. While it offers greater flexibility in configuring each stage compared to managed file searching, the stage configuration follows a predefined structure established by the service.

items.title: Managed service portfolio: Gemini Enterprise, Vector Search, AlloyDB
items.body: Google's reference architecture presents several combinations. Gemini Enterprise and Agent Platform provide managed data stores and agent orchestration. Vector Search offers a fully managed serverless search scaled for large workloads, while AlloyDB for PostgreSQL or Cloud SQL store vector embeddings alongside operational data. As the number of configurable components increases, so does the responsibility for integration and operations.

items.title: GKE-based open-source setup: Maximum control
items.body: The GKE and Cloud SQL-based setup offers a flexible containerized architecture that allows direct application development using open-source tools like Ray, Hugging Face, and LangChain, providing the highest level of control. You can define all aspects including splitting, embedding models, search logic, and permission filtering. However, you are responsible directly for deployment, scaling, monitoring, and incident response.

items.title: GraphRAG: Advanced Configuration with Knowledge Graphs
items.body: GraphRAG is an advanced RAG configuration that combines knowledge graph queries with vector search to retrieve contextually connected data. In Google's reference architecture, an example using Spanner Graph is introduced. It is well-suited for use cases where relationships between documents are important, but it adds the burden of creating and maintaining the graph.

items.title: Common principle: The more options available, the greater the control and responsibility becomes.
items.body: In managed file search, as I move from RAG Engine to managed composition, direct open-source setup, and GraphRAG, the number of components I have to select increases. The more components I choose, the greater the level of control, but also the more operational overhead I must manage. Therefore, it is safer to first determine the required level of control, and then select the lightest possible configuration that matches that level.

screens.outro: Let's compare this difference by operational responsibility item.

screens.title: Comparison of Operational Responsibility and Control Levels
screens.lead: Switch between the two state buttons to compare who is responsible for managing versus directly provisioning the same item.

states.label: Managed File Search
states.body: The partitioning approach uses the provider's default settings and allows adjustment only within the provided configuration range. Index updates occur on a file upload or deletion basis and are handled by the provider. Authorization separation follows a default design that partitions the store by department and connects only the relevant store during queries, and can be further refined using the provided metadata filters. Monitoring and incident response are primarily the provider's responsibility. As a result, deployment is fast and requires minimal operational staff, but it cannot address requirements outside the provided scope. For example, if the default partitioning finely splits tables or clauses such that queries fail, and the provided settings fail to resolve the issue, there is no feasible workaround. Whether requirements fall within this scope is the first criterion for determining whether a managed approach is appropriate.

states.label: Build your own RAG
states.body: The deployment approach is tailored to the document structure, and I define both the embedding model and the search algorithm accordingly. I design and operate a pipeline that detects changes and reprocesses only the modified documents during index updates. Authorization separation involves verifying user permissions at search time, implementing filtering conditions directly, and integrating with internal authorization systems. Monitoring and incident response are also my responsibility. As a result, control levels are maximized, but the development period, operational staff requirements, and incident accountability all increase. For instance, if index updates fail in the early morning, I must diagnose the root cause and restore functionality; additionally, whenever I switch the embedding model, I must personally manage the reprocessing of all documents. Therefore, direct construction is chosen only when strict control is absolutely required.

screens.outro: Let's apply the comparison results to the department-level access control examples.

screens.title: Case Study on Departmental Document Access Separation
screens.lead: The instructor will walk through the process of selecting a method for document access separation by department. Select an arrow to proceed step by step according to the judgment order.

steps.title: Requirement: Documents from other departments must not be mixed.
steps.body: Assume that personnel, financial, and sales documents are separated by department, and that mixed documents from other departments should not appear in search results. Currently, in a managed file search, all documents are uploaded to a single repository. Simply instructing through a prompt to not mention documents from other departments does not guarantee compliance. Filtering must occur at the search results stage.

steps.title: Step 1: Requirement Decomposition: What controls are needed?
steps.body: Controls are divided into three categories: whether separation is done by department during the storage phase, whether filtering by conditions occurs during retrieval, and whether audit logs recording who viewed which document are required. The subsequent assessment depends on which of these requirements are present.

steps.title: Step 2. Managerial Review: Can the store be divided to meet requirements?
steps.body: Create a separate store for each department, and when a query is made, connect only the store corresponding to the user's department, thereby excluding documents from other departments from search results. First, verify whether this design satisfies the requirements. If separation at the store level is sufficient, it is simplest to maintain the existing management model.

steps.title: Step 3. Boundary Judgment: Is a more granular permission required?
steps.body: Within the same department, if permissions differ by document or item, or are assigned based on internal groups and job hierarchies, then store separation alone is insufficient. Check whether the attribute filters provided by the management model can express these rules; if not, then the system has reached its limit.

steps.title: Step 4. Decision: Manage if simple, build directly if detailed.
steps.body: Maintain a department-level separation with a managed approach. If fine-grained control, integration with internal authorization systems, or audit logging is required, transition to a custom-built solution and implement filtering at the search time. After migration, control overhead increases, but responsibilities for partitioning, indexing updates, monitoring, and incident response become fully your responsibility—thus, operational staff and accountability must be planned and coordinated accordingly.

screens.outro: Summarize the key points at the final screen.

screens.title: Operational overhead and control levels are swapped.
screens.lead: This lesson's key points are summarized. Please review your answers to the questions posed in the problem presentation screen.

paragraphs: Managed file search only requires managing files and storage, with segmentation, embedding, indexing, and search handled by the provider. It starts quickly and has light operational overhead, but the control scope is limited. Building it from scratch involves designing and operating every stage myself. While control is the highest, both development time and operational responsibility increase significantly. Combining a RAG Engine with a managed service places it in the middle of this spectrum.

Permission separation must be implemented through storage structure and search filtering, not guaranteed by prompt instructions. Simple department-level separation may be sufficient to achieve by splitting the store and connecting only the relevant store when querying. For fine-grained permissions or internal authorization systems at the document or item level, direct implementation of filtering at the search time is required.

Going back to the initial question, departmental separation can be implemented in two ways: where documents are stored and what is filtered during searches. The latter becomes more significant as requirements become more detailed. One can start with a managed approach and transition to a custom-built solution as control requirements increase. The key is to first identify the necessary controls and then select the lightest possible method to satisfy them. Following this order helps avoid both overbuilding and underbuilding.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The department-level separation examples in the main text are hypothetical assumptions for illustrative purposes. The scope of settings and filters provided by managed services varies by provider; therefore, first verify whether your requirements fall within that scope.

glossary.def: This is a hosting search tool that provides segmentation, embedding, indexing, and search, with the provider handling these processes.
A service that bundles and provides managed functionality for the RAG pipeline stages of collection, transformation, embedding, indexing, and search.
This is a method where you directly select and assemble components such as vector databases, embeddings, and search logic, then operate them.
A design that divides the document scope visible in searches by user or department.

misconceptions.myth: With managed mode, all controls are possible.
misconceptions.fact: In management mode, control is possible only within the settings and filter scope that the provider has established. Requirements outside this scope—such as fine-grained permissions or integration with internal systems—may require direct implementation.
Control is always involved, along with the personnel responsible for setup and operations, and incident response. The lightest approach that satisfies necessary controls is the best.

misconceptions.myth: Permission separation can be blocked by prompt.
misconceptions.fact: Permissions should be filtered at the search results stage. Simply relying on prompt instructions does not guarantee that documents from other departments will not be mixed in.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Operational overhead and control levels are mutually exchanged.
The managed version starts quickly, and the direct setup involves me designing and operating the entire process.
Authorization separation is implemented through storage structure and search filters, and the level of granularity required determines the approach.
You can start with a managed approach and transition to a self-built setup as control requirements increase.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What controls are absolutely necessary to meet my requirements, and to what extent am I responsible for operating those controls?
